ODU_133_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity (c. 11th–14th century CE): Codified at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as Ọ̀kànràn-Túá, establishing divine covenants, release from captivity, and protection of travelers. Imperial Era: Consulted during peace treaty negotiations between Ọ̀yọ́ and regional kingdoms. Diaspora Retention: Maintained in Cuban and Brazilian Ifá archives as Okanran Tura, celebrated for turning conflict into reconciliation.
ODU_133_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (II/II/II/I: moral conscience, thunder voice) on the right and Òtúá (I/II/I/I: spiritual release, light, covenant) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically balances stern judicial resolve with the illuminating mercy of divine prayer, teaching that genuine reconciliation requires uncompromising truth paired with generous grace.
ODU_133_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúá.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn on Ọpọ́n Ifá as II/II/II/I on the right and I/II/I/I on the left. Involves cooling shea butter (Òrí), Ewé Ẹfun, Ewé Tètè, white dove, honey, and white chalk (Ẹfun).
ODU_133_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúá.social_and_ritual_context: Divined during bitter boundary or treaty disputes, release from false accusations, and personal prayers for spiritual deliverance.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn tú okùn ìjà, ó fi àlàáfíà wọ ìlú. (Ọ̀kànràn untied the cords of discord and ushered peace into the town: Sincere prayer and honest speech dissolve ancient grievances.)

Àdúrà olódodo kì í ṣubú sílẹ̀; ìmọ́lẹ̀ òtítọ́ ló ń lé òkùnkùn sá. (The prayer of the righteous never falls to the earth; the light of truth dispels all darkness: Unyielding moral integrity guarantees divine vindication.)
ODU_133_Ọ̀kànràn_Òtúá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.

ODU_134_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrẹtẹ̀.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Tẹtẹ́ or Ọ̀kànràn-Ìrẹtẹ̀, governing the trampling of chronic disease, surgical victory, and bodily purification. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted by military surgeons before and after campaigns. Transatlantic Retention: Retained in Lucumí Ifá as Okanran Rete, presiding over medicinal herbal baths and skin cures.
ODU_134_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrẹtẹ̀.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (judgment, righteous voice) and Ìrẹtẹ̀ (trampling down disease, purification, carving). Teaches that societal and physical maladies cannot be wished away; they must be actively confronted, excised, and trampled underfoot through disciplined medicinal knowledge.
ODU_134_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrẹtẹ̀.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and I/I/II/I on left. Involves Ewé Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ewé Ṣaworo, sulfur-chalk infusions, and consecrated palm oil.
ODU_134_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrẹtẹ̀.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for chronic ailments, post-surgical recovery, and community cleansing rites following pestilential outbreaks.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn tẹ àrùn mọ́lẹ̀, ó fi ìlera fún ará ìlú. (Ọ̀kànràn trampled disease underfoot and endowed the community with health: Active discipline and herbal mastery conquer physical affliction.)
Bí a kò bá tẹ orí ejò mọ́lẹ̀, a kì í rí ojú ọ̀nà tọ́. (Unless one steps firmly upon the serpent's head, the pathway remains hazardous: Bold and decisive action is required against insidious harm.)
ODU_134_Ọ̀kànràn_Ìrẹtẹ̀.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Oliver-Bever, B. (1986). Medicinal Plants in Tropical West Africa.

ODU_135_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Ṣẹ́, the synthesis of judicial righteousness and riverine beauty under Ọ̀ṣun. Imperial Era: Consulted by royal goldsmiths, brass artisans, and court singers. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Cuban Cabildos as Okanran She, unlocking artistic inspiration and victory over financial depression.
ODU_135_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (voice of thunder) and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (victory through joy, sweetness, Ọ̀ṣun's fertility). Teaches that the ultimate vindication of truth is not destructive vengeance, but the flourishing of beauty, artistic harmony, and communal joy.
ODU_135_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and I/II/I/II on left. Prepared with pure honey, Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, yellow chalk, bronze bells, and river stones.
ODU_135_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for artists, musicians, traders, and individuals seeking matrimonial joy and release from sorrow.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn bu oyin sí ẹjọ́, ó sọ ìbànújẹ́ di ayọ̀. (Ọ̀kànràn poured honey upon the dispute and turned sorrow into song: Grace and sweet diplomacy disarm the fiercest adversaries.)

Omi Ọ̀ṣun kì í dọ̀tí kí ó má ṣe mu; ore Ọlọ́run kọjá ìmọ̀ ènìyàn. (The river of Ọ̀ṣun is never too foul to drink; divine benevolence surpasses mortal calculations: Generosity and faith restore abundant life.)
ODU_135_Ọ̀kànràn_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Badejo, Diedre L. (1996). Ọ̀ṣun Ṣèègèsí; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.

ODU_136_Ọ̀kànràn_Òfún.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀kànràn-Fún, concluding the Ọ̀kànràn cycle with Obàtálá's white cloth covenant and elder wisdom. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted when veteran warrior chiefs retired from frontlines into the council of elders. Diaspora Survival: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Okanran Fun, commanding stainless moral integrity.
ODU_136_Ọ̀kànràn_Òfún.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀kànràn (fiery conscience) and Òfún (white chalk, primal purity, senior creation). Demonstrates that fiery martial energy must culminate in the cool, stainless whiteness of elder wisdom and patient character.
ODU_136_Ọ̀kànràn_Òfún.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/II/II/I on right and II/I/II/I on left. Involves pure white cloth (Aṣọ Funfun), white chalk (Ẹfun), shea butter, and cold spring water offerings to Obàtálá.
ODU_136_Ọ̀kànràn_Òfún.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for elder statesmen, high judges, and leaders stepping into supreme ancestral responsibilities.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn wọ aṣọ funfun, ó fi ìwà àgbà dábò bo ìlú. (Ọ̀kànràn donned the white robe and sheltered the community with elder character: Reverent maturity and calm character outweigh raw martial force.)

A kì í fi ẹ̀rẹ̀ kùn aṣọ Obàtálá; orúkọ rere ni adé olóye. (One never soils the sacred vestment of Obàtálá with mud; an unblemished reputation is the crown of the sage: Stainless integrity is life's highest achievement.)
ODU_136_Ọ̀kànràn_Òfún.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_137_Ògúndá_Ogbè.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Bèdé, one of the most celebrated chapters of the Ifá corpus, celebrating the clearing of the primordial path for human civilization by Ògún and Ogbè. Imperial Era: Consulted before opening new highways, imperial foundries, and civic infrastructure. Transatlantic Prominence: Widely cited across Lucumí and Candomblé Ketu as Ogunda Bede, governor of iron technology and surgical precision.
ODU_137_Ògúndá_Ogbè.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (I/I/I/II: iron, toolmaking, cutting edge) on the right and Ogbè (I/I/I/I: pristine light, expansive destiny) on the left. Dialectically represents the technological breakthrough where raw physical nature is opened to human cultivation, commerce, and divine wisdom through courageous labor.
ODU_137_Ògúndá_Ogbè.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed on Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/I/II on right and I/I/I/I on left. Involves forged iron implements, Ewé Pèrègún, Ewé Ọ́kìkà, palm oil, roasted yam, and a rooster offered at Ògún's anvil.
ODU_137_Ògúndá_Ogbè.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when embarking on major construction projects, opening new commercial avenues, conducting complex surgical operations, and inaugurating industrial enterprises.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá Bèdé la ọ̀nà fún gbogbo ayé; irin kì í kọ iṣẹ́ nínú igbó. (Ògúndá Bèdé opened the highway for all the world; forged iron never shirks from labor in the thicket: Industrious labor and technological courage conquer all wilderness.)

Ọ̀bẹ tí ń gbé'lé kì í jẹ koríko; aṣáájú rere ló ń kọ́ ọ̀nà ọlá. (The domestic knife does not feed on weeds; a righteous pioneer is who carves the highway of majesty: Leadership requires forward-thinking action.)
ODU_137_Ògúndá_Ogbè.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.

ODU_138_Ògúndá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Yẹ̀kú, governing the avoidance of violent death, industrial safety, and protective metallurgy. Imperial Era: Consulted by blacksmith guilds before smelting toxic ores and by cavalry commanders before border patrols. Diaspora Tradition: Retained in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Yeku.
ODU_138_Ògúndá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron, warfare) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness, mortality, ancestral veil). Teaches that the destructive potential of metallurgical and martial force must be constantly moderated by solemn ancestral reverence and strict occupational safety.
ODU_138_Ògúndá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/II/II/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Òdúndún, Ewé Rinrin, black cloth, he-goat, and cold water poured over blacksmith anvils.
ODU_138_Ògúndá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to avert industrial accidents, surgical catastrophes, and vehicular mishaps, establishing protective sanctuary for laborers.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá yẹ̀ ikú lórí alágbẹ̀dẹ; a kì í fi irin bọ́ sí kòtò ikú. (Ògúndá averted death from the blacksmith; one does not plunge into the abyss of mortality with iron in hand: Prudent caution preserves the master artisan.)

Ẹni tí ó ń gun ẹṣin ogun kò gbọdọ̀ tẹjú mọ́ eré; ìṣọ́ra ni ẹ̀ṣọ́ ológun. (He who rides the warhorse must not fixate on spectacle; vigilant caution is the soldier's truest armor: Foresight and composure neutralize danger.)
ODU_138_Ògúndá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_139_Ògúndá_Ìwòrì.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Wòrì or Ògúndá-Láwẹ́, governing surgical insight, diagnostic medicine, and piercing hidden conspiracies. Imperial Era: Consulted by intelligence scouts and royal interrogators. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Cuba as Ogunda Lawete.
ODU_139_Ògúndá_Ìwòrì.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (decisive cut) and Ìwòrì (deep spiritual clairvoyance). Demonstrates that decisive physical force without spiritual vision is blind brutality; true victory demands piercing diagnostic insight.
ODU_139_Ògúndá_Ìwòrì.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/I/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ìyàyà, Ewé Iná, ram offering, and consecrated water for ocular purification.
ODU_139_Ògúndá_Ìwòrì.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during forensic investigations, complex medical diagnoses, and detecting hidden palace sabotage.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá fi ojú Ìwòrì wo ogun, ó rí àṣírí ọ̀tá. (Ògúndá surveyed the battle through the eyes of Ìwòrì and uncovered the enemy's secret: Spiritual clarity outmaneuvers raw physical strength.)

A kì í fi ojú lásán wo awo; òye inú ló ń mú idà gé ohun tí ó wọ́. (One does not behold the mysteries with superficial eyes; inner discernment empowers the sword to sever crooked entanglements: True mastery unites vision with action.)
ODU_139_Ògúndá_Ìwòrì.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba.

ODU_140_Ògúndá_Òdí.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Dí, governing iron ramparts, border fortifications, and maternal protection of warrior children. Imperial Era: Consulted during city-wall engineering projects in Ọ̀yọ́, Ìjẹ̀bú, and Abẹ́òkúta. Diaspora Tradition: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Di.
ODU_140_Ògúndá_Òdí.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron strength) and Òdí (protective wall, womb). Teaches that physical force must be directed toward defending homes, sheltering vulnerable citizens, and maintaining civic stability.
ODU_140_Ògúndá_Òdí.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Gbégbé, forged iron spikes, rooster, and fresh palm fronds (Mọ̀rìwò) placed at fortress gates.
ODU_140_Ògúndá_Òdí.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when securing settlements against banditry, defending households from harassment, and safeguarding pregnant women.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá dí odi pẹ̀lú irin; olè kì í ya ilé tí a fi àṣẹ mọ. (Ògúndá fortified the rampart with iron; thieves never breach the compound constructed with divine mandate: Fortified boundaries preserve civic peace.)

Ògiri tí awo kọ́ kì í wó mọ́ ọmọdé lórí; ààbò Ọlọ́run kọjá idà. (The wall constructed by the initiate never collapses upon the youth; divine shelter surpasses the mortal sword: Spiritual protection is an indestructible fortress.)
ODU_140_Ògúndá_Òdí.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_141_Ògúndá_Ìrosùn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Rosùn or Ògúndá-Kósùn, governing the consecration of weapons with camwood, healing battlefield trauma, and purifying bloodlines. Imperial Era: Consulted by warrior guilds returning from war. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Cuba as Ogunda Koso.
ODU_141_Ògúndá_Ìrosùn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron, warfare) and Ìrosùn (camwood, ancestral blood). Teaches that the trauma and bloodshed of warfare must be ritually cleansed through camwood purification and ethical reintegration into peaceful society.
ODU_141_Ògúndá_Ìrosùn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and I/I/II/II on left. Prepared with scarlet Osùn powder, Ewé Àkòko, rooster, and consecrated palm wine.
ODU_141_Ògúndá_Ìrosùn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for veterans, trauma recovery, resolving ancestral family curses, and consecrating ceremonial blades.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá wẹ idà nù pẹ̀lú osùn; a kì í gbé ogun wọlé ayọ̀. (Ògúndá cleansed the blade with sacred camwood; one does not bring the fury of warfare into the house of joy: Purification after conflict restores domestic harmony.)

Ẹ̀jẹ̀ kò gbọdọ̀ ba aṣọ àlàárì jẹ́; ìwà tútù ni oògùn ìbínú. (Blood must not defile the noble crimson garment; gentle character is the antidote to rage: Restraint and reconciliation heal ancient wounds.)
ODU_141_Ògúndá_Ìrosùn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_142_Ògúndá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Wọ́nrín, governing sudden technological windfalls, navigating commercial storms, and breaking weapon-traps. Imperial Era: Consulted before long-distance merchant expeditions. Diaspora Tradition: Preserved in Lucumí as Ogunda Lenikue.
ODU_142_Ògúndá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron resolve, skill) and Ọ̀wọ́nrín (whirlwind, sudden reversal). Teaches that technological and martial power must remain agile and adaptable; rigidity in the face of changing circumstances invites disaster.
ODU_142_Ògúndá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/II/I/I on left. Involves Ewé Àjídèwe, iron filings, pigeon offering, and cowries deposited at a busy crossroads.
ODU_142_Ògúndá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during volatile market crises, sudden trade reversals, and resolving complex technical obstacles.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Afẹ́fẹ́ Ògúndá fẹ́ ewu dànù; olóye kì í fọwọ́ rọ́kú nígbà tí ìjì bá dé. (The gale of Ògúndá blew danger away; the prudent statesman does not panic when the tempest descends: Adaptability and resolve conquer crisis.)

Irin tó gbọ́n ní ń tẹríba fún iná; ìrẹ̀lẹ̀ ló ń sọ líle di dídára. (The wise iron bows before the forge flame; humility is what transforms rigidity into master craftsmanship: Flexibility under trial produces enduring beauty.)
ODU_142_Ògúndá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_143_Ògúndá_Ọ̀bàrà.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Bàrà, governing the synthesis of technological manufacture and royal commerce, transforming forged tools into national wealth. Imperial Era: Consulted by royal treasurers and blacksmith guild masters. Diaspora Lineage: Retained in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Bara.
ODU_143_Ògúndá_Ọ̀bàrà.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron, labor) and Ọ̀bàrà (wealth, nobility, eloquence). Proves that durable national prosperity does not come from passive inheritance, but from skilled industrial manufacturing, ethical commerce, and rewarding craftsmanship.
ODU_143_Ògúndá_Ọ̀bàrà.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and I/II/II/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ajé, Ewé Pèrègún, pigeon, honey, and sixteen consecrated cowries placed near the forge.
ODU_143_Ògúndá_Ọ̀bàrà.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for engineers, manufacturers, traders, and entrepreneurs seeking financial expansion through productive industries.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá pọn idà, Ọ̀bàrà mú owó wọlé; iṣẹ́ ọwọ́ awo kì í di asán. (Ògúndá sharpened the blade, and Ọ̀bàrà brought riches into the home; skilled handiwork never turns to vanity: Productive industry is the foundation of wealth.)

A kì í fi ọ̀lẹ gbé adé ọlá; ọwọ́ tí ó ń ṣiṣẹ́ ni Ọlọ́run ń bùkún. (One does not attain the crown of majesty through indolence; the working hand is what the Almighty blesses: Diligent enterprise guarantees lasting honor.)
ODU_143_Ògúndá_Ọ̀bàrà.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Falola, Toyin (1984). The Political Economy of a Pre-colonial African State.

ODU_144_Ògúndá_Ọ̀kànràn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Kànràn, governing judicial enforcement of truth, military resistance against tyrants, and judicial duel verdicts. Imperial Era: Consulted during treason tribunals in Ọ̀yọ́. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Ogunda Kana.
ODU_144_Ògúndá_Ọ̀kànràn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (sword, executive action) and Ọ̀kànràn (voice of moral conscience). Teaches that the sword of justice must never strike without moral cause, and that executive force is illegitimate when divorced from truth.
ODU_144_Ògúndá_Ọ̀kànràn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/II/II/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ́kìkà, Ewé Iná, ram to Ṣàngó and Ògún, and fresh kola nuts.
ODU_144_Ògúndá_Ọ̀kànràn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during bitter litigation, uncovering systemic corruption, and defending innocent parties against tyrannical bullies.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Idà Ògúndá kì í gé orí olódodo; Ọ̀kànràn ló ń fọhùn òtítọ́. (The sword of Ògúndá never severs the head of the righteous; Ọ̀kànràn is the voice of truth: Justice and truth defend the innocent against malice.)

A kì í fi agbára gba ẹ̀tọ́ ọmọdé; ẹni tí ó ba lo idà láìtọ́ yóò rí ìdájọ́. (One does not seize the rights of the vulnerable through sheer might; he who wields the blade unlawfully shall face cosmic judgment: Power without righteousness consumes its master.)
ODU_144_Ògúndá_Ọ̀kànràn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun.

ODU_145_Ògúndá_Ọ̀sá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Mása, governing the reconciliation between blacksmiths and the mystical Mothers (Ìyàmi Òṣòròngà). Imperial Era: Consulted before smelting campaigns to ensure spiritual equilibrium. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Masa.
ODU_145_Ògúndá_Ọ̀sá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron, male martial strength) and Ọ̀sá (flight, storm winds, sacred female mysteries). Teaches that technological and military might cannot subjugate the mysterious feminine and cosmic forces; wisdom bows and placates through respectful diplomacy.
ODU_145_Ògúndá_Ọ̀sá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, Ewé Tètè-tútù, shea butter, cold water, and white chalk.
ODU_145_Ògúndá_Ọ̀sá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to defuse fierce community wrath, calm psychological panic, and pacify spiritual hostility from the Mothers of the Night.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá sá fún ìjà, ó fi ọgbọ́n ra ẹ̀mí; akíkanjú tí ó gbọ́n kì í kú lásán. (Ògúndá retreated from futile strife and redeemed life through wisdom; the courageous hero who is prudent never perishes in vain: Strategic retreat and humble diplomacy preserve life.)

Irin líle kì í bá afẹ́fẹ́ jà; ẹni tí ó mọ̀ bí a ti ń tẹríba kì í fọ́. (Hardened iron does not contend with the tempest; he who knows how to bow never breaks: True strength accommodates higher cosmic orders.)
ODU_145_Ògúndá_Ọ̀sá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. (1992). Gelede: Art and Female Power.

ODU_146_Ògúndá_Ìká.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Ká, governing the severing of malicious nets, breaking criminal conspiracies, and exposing traitorous comrades. Imperial Era: Consulted by palace guards detecting infiltration. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Ogunda Ka.
ODU_146_Ògúndá_Ìká.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (cleaving blade) and Ìká (wicked cord, snare). Teaches that covert entrapments and malicious legal traps are shattered when confronted with decisive, fearless truth.
ODU_146_Ògúndá_Ìká.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/I/II/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ègé, Ewé Arújẹ, white pigeon, and a severed cord signifying liberation.
ODU_146_Ògúndá_Ìká.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for persons ensnared by false contracts, blackmail, or malicious judicial entrapments.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá gé okùn ìkà, ó fi òmìnira fún awo; kòtò tí ọ̀tá gbẹ́ ni yóò wọ̀. (Ògúndá severed the cord of malice and granted freedom to the initiate; the pit dug by the adversary shall swallow him: Treacherous snares inevitably trap their architects.)

A kì í fi ọwọ́ mú iná jẹun; idà òtítọ́ ló ń tu àwọn alárékérekè ká. (One does not feast with burning coals in hand; the sword of truth scatters the duplicitous: Integrity shatters clandestine conspiracies.)
ODU_146_Ògúndá_Ìká.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.

ODU_147_Ògúndá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Túúrúpọ̀n, governing pediatric resilience, protective childcare for artisans, and safe obstetrics. Imperial Era: Consulted by royal midwives and pediatric healers. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Trupon.
ODU_147_Ògúndá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (protection, strength) and Òtúúrúpọ̀n (maternal care, carrying infants upon the back). Demonstrates that the true nobility of strength is deployed in sheltering fragile infants and nurturing the next generation.
ODU_147_Ògúndá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/II/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀já-Ọmọ, Ewé Àbáwẹ̀, snail broth, shea butter, and cold maize pap.
ODU_147_Ògúndá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for pregnant mothers, sick infants, and families building generational health.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá fi agbára pọ̀n ọmọ mọ́ra; agbára tí kò dáàbò bo ọmọdé jẹ́ asán. (Ògúndá strapped the infant to the back with protective strength; power that fails to defend children is vanity: Strength must serve generational preservation.)

Ẹrù ọmọ kì í pa ìyá; ìfẹ́ inú ló ń kọ́ ọmọdé ní ọ̀nà ìyè. (The burden of an infant never wearies the mother; deep love guides the child onto the path of life: Nurturing care secures the commonwealth.)
ODU_147_Ògúndá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_148_Ògúndá_Òtúá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Túá or Ògúndá-Tẹtútú, governing military disarmament, inter-state treaties, and the blessing of peaceful commerce. Imperial Era: Consulted when ratifying peace treaties between kingdoms. Diaspora Survival: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Tura.
ODU_148_Ògúndá_Òtúá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (weapons of war) and Òtúá (prayer, release, covenant). Teaches that the highest achievement of military strength is establishing lasting peace, transforming swords into plowshares.
ODU_148_Ògúndá_Òtúá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and I/II/I/I on left. Involves Ewé Ẹfun, Ewé Tètè-Àgbalagba, honey, white dove, and white chalk (Ẹfun).
ODU_148_Ògúndá_Òtúá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during treaty signings, resolving bitter business partnerships, and prayers for cessation of armed conflict.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá tú ìhámọ́ ogun sílẹ̀, ó fi àdúrà gba ìlú; àlàáfíà kọjá idà. (Ògúndá disassembled the armaments of war and delivered the city through prayer; peace surpasses the blade: Sacred reconciliation is superior to endless bloodshed.)

Àdúrà àlàáfíà ló ń mú ìlú gbilẹ̀; ẹni tí ó ba gbé ogun ga yóò rí ìbànújẹ́. (The prayer for peace causes the commonwealth to flourish; he who exalts war shall reap sorrow: Lasting honor belongs to peacemakers.)
ODU_148_Ògúndá_Òtúá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Law, Robin (1977). The Oyo Empire.

ODU_149_Ògúndá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Kẹtẹ̀ or Ògúndá-Ìrẹtẹ̀, governing victory over viral skin pestilence, surgical incisions, and public hygiene. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal epidemic quarantines. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Ogunda Kete.
ODU_149_Ògúndá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (cutting blade) and Ìrẹtẹ̀ (carving away rot, bodily purification). Demonstrates that toxic corruption and disease must be excised surgically and cleanly without sentimental compromise.
ODU_149_Ògúndá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and I/I/II/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ewé Ṣaworo, sulfur bath, and cold shea butter ointment.
ODU_149_Ògúndá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for surgical procedures, treating chronic ulcers, and community health purifications.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá rẹ àrùn kúrò lára awo; ìmọ́tótó ni àbò ẹ̀mí. (Ògúndá excised sickness from the initiate's body; cleanliness is the shield of life: Decisive surgical hygiene restores wholeness.)
Bí a kò bá bẹ́ ibi tí ó wọ́ dànù, a kì í rí ibi tútù simi. (Unless one lops off the infected branch, the tree finds no peaceful rest: Resolute elimination of corruption preserves the body.)
ODU_149_Ògúndá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_150_Ògúndá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Ṣẹ́, governing artistic metallurgy, casting sacred brass bells (Aago), and victory through joyous celebration. Imperial Era: Consulted by master bronze casters of Ifẹ̀ and Ọ̀yọ́. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Cuba as Ogunda She.
ODU_150_Ògúndá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (metal casting) and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (victory through sweetness, Ọ̀ṣun). Teaches that raw metallurgy attains its pinnacle when forged into musical instruments, temple bells, and sacred art that elevate the spirit.
ODU_150_Ògúndá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and I/II/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, wild honey, cast bronze bell, and yellow cloth.
ODU_150_Ògúndá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for bronze casters, sculptors, and musicians seeking artistic breakthroughs and commercial success.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá kọ agogo idẹ, ó fi orin ayọ̀ wọlé; iṣẹ́ ọnà ló ń gbé awo ga. (Ògúndá forged the bronze bell and entered with songs of joy; master art elevates the initiate: Creative excellence sanctifies material labor.)

Oyin dídùn kì í korò; ẹni tí ó ba fi ìmọ́lẹ̀ ọnà kẹ́ ayé yóò rí ẹ̀yẹ gbà. (Sweet honey never turns bitter; he who graces the world with artistic light shall receive enduring honor: Beauty outlasts violence.)
ODU_150_Ògúndá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Williams, Denis (1974). Icon and Image.

ODU_151_Ògúndá_Òfún.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ògúndá-Fún, concluding the Ògúndá cycle with Obàtálá's white cloth purity and peaceful elder retirement. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted when aging master blacksmiths passed their sacred anvils to their eldest sons. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Lucumí as Ogunda Fun.
ODU_151_Ògúndá_Òfún.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ògúndá (iron strength) and Òfún (white chalk, elder purity). Teaches that the true conclusion of all material and martial labor is honorable rest, spotless reputation, and spiritual alignment with the Creator.
ODU_151_Ògúndá_Òfún.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I/I/I/II on right and II/I/II/I on left. Involves pure white cloth, white chalk (Ẹfun), shea butter, cold spring water, and a white pigeon.
ODU_151_Ògúndá_Òfún.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for retiring master craftsmen, veteran leaders, and elders seeking longevity and spotless honor.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògúndá fi aṣọ funfun bo idà mọ́lẹ̀; ìsinmi olódodo kún fún àbùkún. (Ògúndá cloaked the blade beneath spotless white cloth; the retirement of the righteous is crowned with blessing: Peaceful elder character transcends physical battle.)

Àgbà tí ó ní sùúrù ló ń jẹ adé ọlá; ìwà tútù ni òpin gbogbo agbára. (The elder who masters patience inherits the crown of majesty; gentle character is the fulfillment of all strength: Moral elevation crowns life's labors.)
ODU_151_Ògúndá_Òfún.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_152_Ọ̀sá_Ogbè.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀sá-Ogbè or Ọ̀sá-Lufun, opening the sacred Ọ̀sá cycle, governing astral travel, spiritual diplomacy with the Mothers of the Night, and the dawning of mystical revelation. Imperial Era: Consulted before major nocturnal assemblies and palace coronation watches. Diaspora Prominence: Celebrated in Lucumí and Candomblé Ketu as Osa Lofobeyo, governing spiritual protection from witchcraft.
ODU_152_Ọ̀sá_Ogbè.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀sá (II/I/I/I: the mystical wind, flight, Ìyàmi) on the right and Ogbè (I/I/I/I: solar light, opening highway) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically represents the illuminating dawn piercing nocturnal storms, teaching that mystical knowledge must serve constructive moral enlightenment rather than terror.
ODU_152_Ọ̀sá_Ogbè.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed on Ọpọ́n Ifá as II/I/I/I on right and I/I/I/I on left. Prepared with Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, Ewé Tètè-tútù, shea butter, white chalk, white dove, and egg offerings.
ODU_152_Ọ̀sá_Ogbè.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during profound existential uncertainty, night terrors, and seeking spiritual alliances with ancestral matriarchs.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀sá la ojú fún Ogbè, ìmọ́lẹ̀ fẹ́ òkùnkùn dànù. (Ọ̀sá opened the eye for Ogbè, and light banished darkness: Spiritual insight transforms mysterious forces into divine revelation.)

Afẹ́fẹ́ kì í jà kí ó fọ́ ọpọ́n Ifá; awo tí ó ní ìrẹ̀lẹ̀ kì í rì nínú ìjì. (The storm wind never shatters the divination tray; the initiate clothed in humility never drowns in the gale: Reverent character guarantees safe passage through spiritual turbulence.)
ODU_152_Ọ̀sá_Ogbè.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. (1992). Gelede: Art and Female Power among the Yoruba.

ODU_153_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀sá-Yẹ̀kú, governing the pacification of catastrophic cyclones, ancestral nocturnal defense, and averting plagues. Imperial Era: Consulted during devastating windstorms that unroofed royal compounds. Diaspora Tradition: Preserved in Lucumí as Osa Yeku.
ODU_153_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀sá (tempest, flight) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness, mortality, ancestral veil). Teaches that the terrifying convergence of storm and shadow can only be calmed through deep ancestral pacification and humble libation.
ODU_153_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/I/I/I on right and II/II/II/II on left. Involves Ewé Òdúndún, Ewé Rinrin, black cloth, he-goat, and cold water poured upon ancestral earthen altars.
ODU_153_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to avert sudden communal epidemics, catastrophic storms, and nocturnal curses.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀sá yẹ̀ ikú lórí awo, ó fi omi tútù paná ìjì. (Ọ̀sá averted death from the initiate's head, quenching the storm with cool water: Calm character and timely libation pacify cosmic wrath.)

A kì í fi ìbínú bá afẹ́fẹ́ jà; sùúrù ló ń tọ́jú ẹ̀mí nínú ewu. (One does not contend with the howling wind in fury; patience preserves life amid peril: Composure is the antidote to existential panic.)
ODU_153_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_154_Ọ̀sá_Ìwòrì.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀sá-Wòrì or Ọ̀sá-Wó, governing clairvoyant dream interpretation, prophetic foresight, and detecting unseen traps. Imperial Era: Consulted by royal dream diviners in the Aláàfin's court. Diaspora Lineage: Retained in Cuba as Osa Wo.
ODU_154_Ọ̀sá_Ìwòrì.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀sá (flight, spirit) and Ìwòrì (deep spiritual seeing). Demonstrates that intuitive dreams and astral visions must be decoded with rigorous philosophical discernment to guide practical civic action.
ODU_154_Ọ̀sá_Ìwòrì.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/I/I/I on right and II/I/I/II on left. Prepared with Ewé Ìyàyà, Ewé Iná, ram offering, and clear spring water for head washing.
ODU_154_Ọ̀sá_Ìwòrì.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for interpreting recurrent dreams, forewarning communities of covert perils, and mental clarity.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀sá wò inú àlá, ó rí ọ̀nà àlàáfíà; ojú awo kì í sùn nínú ewu. (Ọ̀sá gazed into the dream and revealed the path of peace; the eye of the initiate never sleeps in peril: Intuitive foresight safeguards against covert danger.)

Àlá tí ó dọ́gba pẹ̀lú òtítọ́ kì í purọ́; ìtọ́sọ́nà Ọlọ́run ló ń ṣí ojú ẹ̀dá. (The dream aligned with truth never deceives; divine guidance is what opens mortal perception: Spiritual attunement brings clairvoyance.)
ODU_154_Ọ̀sá_Ìwòrì.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba.

ODU_155_Ọ̀sá_Òdí.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀sá-Dí, governing the fortification of the spirit against nocturnal intrusions, womb defense, and maternal fertility. Imperial Era: Consulted by palace matrons protecting pregnant royal wives. Diaspora Tradition: Maintained in Lucumí Ifá as Osa Di.
ODU_155_Ọ̀sá_Òdí.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀sá (wind, spirit) and Òdí (fortress, enclosure). Teaches that the human mind and reproductive sanctum require strong spiritual boundaries to prevent invasive emotional and psychological manipulation.
ODU_155_Ọ̀sá_Òdí.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/I/I/I on right and II/I/I/I on left. Involves Ewé Gbégbé, fresh palm fronds, white pigeon, and cold maize porridge (Ẹ̀kọ).
ODU_155_Ọ̀sá_Òdí.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for protecting expectant mothers, defending households against nightmares, and sealing spiritual boundaries.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀sá dí ojú ọ̀nà fún ibi; afẹ́fẹ́ burúkú kì í fọ́ odi awo. (Ọ̀sá sealed the gateway against malevolence; the foul wind never shatters the fortress of the initiate: Strong spiritual boundaries preserve domestic serenity.)

Ilé tí a fi àṣẹ mọ kì í gba àlejò ibi; àlàáfíà ni adé ìdílé. (The house erected upon sacred mandate admits no destructive intruder; peace is the crown of the family: Moral fortitude guards the hearth.)
ODU_155_Ọ̀sá_Òdí.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_156_Ọ̀sá_Ìrosùn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀sá-Rosùn or Ọ̀sá-Kósùn, governing the purification of bloodlines from mystical afflictions, healing menstrual irregularities, and honoring female ancestors. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal birth blessings. Diaspora Lineage: Preserved in Cuba as Osa Roso.
ODU_156_Ọ̀sá_Ìrosùn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀sá (mystical female wind) and Ìrosùn (camwood, ancestral bloodline). Teaches that the maternal bloodline carries sacred spiritual potency which must be honored through camwood purification and respectful veneration of mothers.
ODU_156_Ọ̀sá_Ìrosùn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/I/I/I on right and I/I/II/II on left. Prepared with scarlet Osùn powder, Ewé Àkòko, rooster, and palm oil.
ODU_156_Ọ̀sá_Ìrosùn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for gynecological healing, honoring female ancestral lines, and removing inherited spiritual curses.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀sá pa osùn kùn ẹ̀jẹ̀ awo, ó sọ àbùkù di ọlá. (Ọ̀sá anointed the initiate's bloodline with camwood, turning dishonor into majesty: Honoring ancestral mothers elevates the lineage to glory.)

Ẹ̀jẹ̀ ìyá ni orísun ẹ̀mí; ẹni tí ó ba bu ọlá fún àwọn ìyá kì í rí ìtìjú. (The mother's blood is the fountain of life; he who honors women never tastes humiliation: Filial reverence brings divine favor.)
ODU_156_Ọ̀sá_Ìrosùn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_157_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀sá-Wọ́nrín or Ọ̀sá-Oníwọ́nrín, governing the whirlwind of commercial fortune, rapid elevation of status, and navigating volatile social storms. Imperial Era: Consulted by international caravan guilds crossing borders. Diaspora Tradition: Retained in Lucumí as Osa Juani.
ODU_157_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀sá (flight, wind) and Ọ̀wọ́nrín (whirlwind, sudden reversal). Teaches that when unpredictable tides of fortune shift rapidly, wisdom anchors itself in moral integrity, avoiding reckless panic or arrogant overconfidence.
ODU_157_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/I/I/I on right and II/II/I/I on left. Involves Ewé Àjídèwe, Ewé Ọlọ́jọ̀bọ́, rooster, and cowrie shells deposited at a crossroads.
ODU_157_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during rapid financial transitions, volatile trade environments, and sudden changes in social or political status.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Afẹ́fẹ́ Ọ̀sá gbé ọrọ̀ wọlé, Ọ̀wọ́nrín sọ ọ́ di púpọ̀. (The wind of Ọ̀sá swept wealth into the compound, and Ọ̀wọ́nrín multiplied it: Sudden fortune requires patient wisdom to yield lasting benefit.)

Ìjì líle kì í gbé olóye lọ; ẹni tí ó dúró lórí òtítọ́ kì í ṣubú. (The ferocious gale never sweeps the wise away; he who stands upon truth never falls: Inner integrity remains unshakeable amidst the storm.)
ODU_157_Ọ̀sá_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.
